title: New malware doesn’t call home, it turns your Exchange server into its home
summary: There’s a new flavor of cereal on the table, but not the appealing kind, particularly for defenders. A new report from global security company ESET describes a “sophisticated, modular, and tightly interconnected” toolset designed to run on compromised Exchange servers for long-term cyberespionage. The malware is named ‘Cereal’ because it relies heavily on serialization, a technique used to package data and code for transport. It comprises a novel Exchange email collection module, a sneaky command and control (C&C) mechanism, and clever .NET execution tricks. While as of now, it is being used by nation-state actors to attack government bodies , enterprises should still be concerned. “Tradecraft like this tends not to stay with its inventors,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research, citing a baseball analogy: “Criminal groups study nation-state techniques the way minor leaguers study a big league pitcher’s grip. What works in the majors eventually shows up in every ballpark.” Sophisticated tradecraft ESET describes Cereal as a malware toolkit that runs on Microsoft Exchange servers, receives commands and executes them in memory, maps the victim organization, and collects selected email messages. No external network infrastructure was identified; instead, the toolkit contains a passive backdoor that runs on targeted servers and provides access. It leaves little on disk. The researchers noted that one of the most interesting aspects of the toolkit is what they did not find: External C&C infrastructure. The victim’s compromised Exchange server is effectively “co-opted” to play the part. Operators send commands as separate, but similarly-structured, executables, suggesting an automated framework. title: The bad news for Microsoft in the Blue Tsunami
summary: Elections have consequences — and big elections have big consequences. Few have been bigger than last week’s US midterms, featuring a Blue Tsunami that swept aside Republican control of Congress and signaled the end of Trumpism. Those consequences will especially be felt by Big Tech and Big AI. Voters made it clear that they don’t want data centers in their backyards. They voted for candidates who vowed to rein in AI, and those who promised to investigate the cozy relationship between tech companies and President Trump. And they voted for candidates who promised to put an end to rampant government corruption tied to tech billionaires. Microsoft didn’t go all-in on Trump as so many Big Tech firms did. The company held fast to core values like diversity, equity, and inclusion in its hiring and employment practices. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella didn’t attend Trump’s inauguration as other tech CEOs including Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, Google’s Sundar Pichai, and Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk did. He didn’t fawn over Trump like Apple’s Tim Cook , who gave Trump a 24-carat gold plaque and attended the gala White House screening of the Amazon-funded Melania documentary held on the day US Immigration and Custom Enforcement (ICE) agents murdered Alex Pretti in Minnesota. Microsoft even fired its law firm because the firm agreed to provide Trump with $125 million in pro bono work, replacing it with a firm that sued Trump. But in other ways, Microsoft has played nice with the Trump administration, including donating millions of dollars for his White House ballroom project. So Microsoft is no more protected than other tech companies against what comes next under the Democratic Congress. In this column I’ll look at the potential bad news for the company. title: Adobe opens Creative Cloud apps to third-party AI assistants
summary: Adobe will open its Creative Cloud applications to third-party AI assistants, with the ability to edit content in Photoshop, After Effects, Illustrator, and Premiere from tools such as ChatGPT or Claude, the company announced at its Max event. The model context protocol (MCP) integration, due in private beta in early 2027, would let third-party AI assistants to make changes to content in Creative Cloud desktop applications, without losing the ability to adjust individual elements of a design or video manually afterwards. For example, a third-party AI assistant could remove a logo from multiple advertising campaign assets. “Make the change once, then ask your agent to cascade it across the rest of the campaign, and step in at any moment to refine the work by hand,” said Deepa Subramaniam, Adobe’s VP, product marketing for Creative Cloud, in a blog post Tuesday. Third-party agents could also connect to other apps in a single workflow, so it would be possible to “pull in a project brief from Google Docs, work on it in Adobe’s tools and share the result with your team via Slack,” for example, Subramaniam said. The MCP connections can help creative professionals “keep their work where they choose to work, without sacrificing the upside of modern collaborative and secure systems,” said Liz Miller, vice president and principal analyst at Constellation Research. “End users … have always relied on multiple tools to capture their taste and bring it to life. title: Explainable deep learning improves human mental models of self-driving cars
summary: How can a passenger understand why a self-driving car behaves unexpectedly? This study introduces the Concept-Wrapper Network (CW-Net), which connects a learned planner to human-readable concepts and examines whether explanations improve understanding of vehicle behaviour. Its evaluation combines private-track experiments with a real autonomous vehicle, expert and non-expert studies, and an online study using public-road recordings collected while a human drove. Participants receiving concept explanations performed better on selected questions about surprising situations. The accompanying critique distinguishes the architecture in which concepts determine the planning reward from an alternative that provides diagnostic explanations without determining trajectory selection. It also examines concept-recognition errors, the inclusion of caution questions in a prediction measure, and uncertainty about effects during ordinary situations. The publication offers evidence about interpretable planning and human understanding, while explaining why these results do not establish safer autonomous operation on public roads or unrestricted replication of the complete vehicle system.

title: AWS unveils local emulator service to help enterprises accelerate app development and testing
summary: AWS launched a new local emulator service for its cloud services on Wednesday to help enterprises accelerate application development and testing. The service, named AWS Emulator, will allow developers and AI coding agents to build, deploy, and test AWS-dependent applications on their machines without provisioning actual cloud infrastructure and paying for it, thereby potentially reducing development time and associated costs, the hyperscaler said in a statement. To achieve this, AWS Emulator replicates the APIs of AWS services locally and exposes a local HTTP endpoint that the AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), software development kits (SDKs), and coding agents can access using the same APIs they use to interact with the cloud, it added. Developers can redirect these tools to the local endpoint by setting the AWS_ENDPOINT_URL environment variable, allowing existing application code and tests to run against simulated AWS services without modification, it further said. Local testing to speed up development The new service addresses a growing problem for developers in software development: the need to test increasingly complex cloud applications quickly and repeatedly without the cost and operational overhead of deploying them to the cloud, said Ashish Chaturvedi , executive research leader at HFS Research. “Developers can test multi-service workflows involving S3 , Lambda , DynamoDB , and API Gateway without provisioning anything, and they avoid both the AWS charges and the clutter of half-finished resources that experiments tend to leave behind in shared accounts,” Chaturvedi said. “I am sure there would be clients that found a forgotten test bucket or idle instance on a cloud bill months later. Such clients will appreciate an environment that vanishes when the work is done,” Chaturvedi added. title: Rewriting less than 10 neurons in an LLM can turn it into a sleeper backdoor
summary: Microsoft researchers have found that rewriting fewer than 10 rarely used neurons in an open-weight AI model can turn any agent built on it into a sleeper backdoor that runs an attacker’s commands on cue, with no retraining required. Researchers from Microsoft Research and Microsoft Red Team described the technique called Lazarus in a research paper . It modifies dormant neurons in a model’s final feed-forward layer to recognize a trigger and inject attacker-controlled commands into the model’s output. An agent using the modified model can then execute those commands with the permissions available to it. “The trigger can be as mundane as a date change, e.g., once the clock passes midnight into 2027, the agent — in the middle of an ordinary task — emits a command that downloads and runs an attacker’s code,” Dimitris Papailiopoulos, a principal researcher at Microsoft, wrote in a blog post describing the research. “The agent then executes it with whatever access you gave it.” Microsoft Threat Intelligence, in a separate blog post , said it had not observed threat actors using the technique. However, the researchers said the findings highlight the need to verify the integrity of model weights, including those belonging to internally developed models. Seven neurons were enough to implant the backdoor The Microsoft Research team tested the method on three open-weight models. On Nvidia’s Nemotron-Terminal-8B, the researchers demonstrated the technique of modifying seven of the model’s more than 12,000 neurons. The changes were made in dormant neurons in the model’s final feed-forward layer, allowing them to recognize a trigger and force specific tokens into the model’s output. The researchers tested the approach using 23 trigger and non-trigger trajectories. The modified model generated the malicious payload in at least 98.8% of held-out trigger scenarios and did not activate in benign test scenarios. title: Claude Code’s ‘don’t ask again’ button has a secrets-spilling problem
summary: A configuration file meant to store local command permissions on Anthropic’s Claude Code is exposing thousands of API keys, database credentials and other secrets, according to findings by GitGuardian. The code security firm identified 31,088 distinct secrets in Claude Code’s “.claude/settings.local.json” files across 23,276 public GitHub repositories. Of those, 5343 were still valid when GitGuardian detected them. The exposed credentials include database connection strings, cloud provider tokens, SSH passwords, Google API keys, and AU service credentials. “Monthly leaks in settings.local.json peaked at 12,535 occurrences in April 2026, then fell to 959 by October, and we do not yet know what changed,” GitGuardian researcher Guillaume Valadon said in a blog post . Apart from source code repositories, the exposure included secrets embedded in publicly accessible Docker Hub images. The problem, Valadon explained, lies with how Claude Code handles command approvals. Command approvals turn into credential storage Claude Code asks developers for permission before executing certain shell commands. When a developer selects the “Yes, and don’t ask again” option, the tool saves an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json, a project-level configuration file. The catch is that the saved rule contains the actual command string, including any credentials embedded in it. For instance, a developer asking Claude Code to interact with an API might approve a curl command containing an API key in its HTTP header. Claude Code then stores that entire command as an approved rule, leaving the credential in the configuration file. Although Claude Code automatically adds the file to its local Git ignore settings, that protection does not necessarily carry over to other machines or repositories, Valadon said. title: Software developers need an Agentic manifesto
summary: I can’t decide whether Agile development is completely dead or about to make a huge comeback. Or maybe Waterfall will. Who knows? Coding agents are changing everything — and I don’t think we’ve quite figured out how they are going to update our methodology, or how we are going to organize ourselves to take advantage of them. We have barely scratched the surface. Folks who have been around a while will remember the Waterfall method for developing software. Because coding was the hardest part of any project, Waterfall called for figuring everything out before you even started writing code. You would write a huge specification, detailing everything, then turn it over to the development team. The development team would build to the spec and pass the software on to the testing team who would verify it, and finally the project would be delivered to customers. Never mind that by the time the thing was built and tested, what the customer wanted had probably changed dramatically. And if the customer decided they wanted a widget here and a sprocket there after the specification was written? Well, that would be a formal change request and would require a whole lot more time and money, thank you very much. Yeah, they really did it that way. Waterfall bad, Agile good It didn’t take long for everyone to figure out that the Waterfall way wasn’t going to cut it. Projects were almost always late and not at all what customers wanted. There had to be a better way, and eventually a bunch of software luminaries quite literally got together in a room and wrote the Agile manifesto . They argued that you didn’t have to be so rigid to actually get things done. It was quite revolutionary at the time . The Agile manifesto helped popularize methods like Scrum and other implementations of Agile, which of course have been much debated. title: MCP and A2A alone won’t scale AI agents
summary: Two protocols define how AI agents connect to internal resources and collaborate with other AI agents. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is well known because it’s promoted as a general protocol for connecting AI agents to resources and other AI agents. But that’s not completely accurate. It’s really the Agent2Agent protocol (A2A) that’s enabling AI agent orchestration . The confusion stems from how quickly platforms have adopted these protocols and marketed them as features. Users building their own AI agents with Claude, OpenAI, Microsoft Copilot, and other models are already being exposed to customizing skills, connectors, and other plug-ins that use MCP and A2A. Vibe coding and AI app-building tools like Bolt.new, Lovable, Pave, Replit, and v0 can connect to MCP servers and include built-in connectors. AI coding editors like Claude Code, Cursor, Devin Desktop, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, and Kiro have MCP clients. These protocols will shape how enterprises scale and manage AI agents. Gartner predicts that the average global Fortune 500 enterprise will run more than 150,000 AI agents over the next two years. But according to Collibra’s 2026 Hallucination Tax Report , 76% have hit critical roadblocks while attempting to move from pilot to full production during the past 12 months. Reviewing the two protocols and which services are your responsibility to layer on top of them is key to scaling enterprise-ready AI agents. Differences between MCP and A2A Scott Gerlach, cofounder and chief security officer at StackHawk , offers this analogy to help technologists better understand MCP and A2A’s functions. “If you think about doing some bathroom remodeling and you call a plumber to move a sink, he’d use tools in his MCP toolbox to complete his work. But when it’s time to fix the drywall, repaint, and put the vanity back together, the plumber agent would use A2A to call other contractor agents to complete that work,” Gerlach says. title: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video
summary: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works. The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs. I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below: We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...] As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention . Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...] The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units.
